title: Testimonials that are allowed to be specific
excerpt: A useful testimonial names the situation and the change. A line that only says the team was great gives a serious buyer nothing to judge.
alt: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table. The person at work fits a piece about quotes that should name a real situation.
caption: A useful line names what changed. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What makes a testimonial useful?
faqs.answer: It names the situation and the change, so the reader learns what kind of project it was and what was different afterward. A sentence that only says the team was responsive can be true and still be impossible for a serious buyer to use. Specific is quotable. Vague is decoration.

faqs.question: How do you ask for one?
faqs.answer: Ask after a real milestone, and ask two questions: what was true before, and what changed. Offer to draft from their answer and let them edit. Do not hand them a glowing paragraph to sign. Tell them the line will carry their name, role, and company, and that they can strike anything.

faqs.question: What if you do not have quotes yet?
faqs.answer: Show the work. A project with a clear caption is better proof than a fabricated or anonymous compliment, and Google's people-first guidance weighs experience and trust more than slogans. Leave the quote area empty until a real person will put their name on a real change. An invented line is a liability the first time someone asks.

markdown:
A useful testimonial names the situation and the change. That is the bar for testimonial design. "Great to work with" cannot be quoted by a serious buyer, because it could sit on any site in the category. They need to know what kind of problem it was, and what was different when the work was done.

You are asking another person to lend you their name. Spend it on a sentence they would still say if a peer asked them in private. If they would not, do not publish it. The layout cannot rescue a line that has no fact in it.

## Situation and change

The situation is the context a buyer recognizes. A first marketing site. A store moving off a platform that was breaking. An editorial project with a long archive. A product with too many screens. The more a prospect can see themselves in the setup, the more the next clause matters. Without the setup, the praise floats.

The change is the outcome in ordinary words. The page became something the team could edit. The checkout survived the move. The archive was readable. The product got down to the screens that mattered. You do not need a percentage you cannot source. A false precision is worse than a plain change. If you have a real number the client will stand behind, use it, and be ready for someone to ask how it was measured.

One or two sentences are enough. A paragraph that retells your whole process in the client's voice usually sounds coached. Let the line be a little plain. Plain sounds like a person. Polish it only to remove your jargon, not to insert your adjectives.

Pair the line with the work when you can. A quote next to the project it describes is stronger than a quote in a carousel far from any evidence. The buyer can look at the thing and the sentence together. If the project cannot be shown, say why in the caption, not in a fog of "a leading brand."

## What to ask, and when

Ask when the work is real and the memory is fresh. The week after launch, or after the first month of them using what you shipped. A request six months later gets a kind, vague reply, because the sharp details have faded and the person is being polite. Polite is how you get "great to work with."

Ask in a way that is easy to answer. Two questions are plenty. What was the situation before we started? What changed that you actually notice? You can add, what should the next client know? Then offer to draft a short line from their words and send it back for a yes, a cut, or a no. Drafting is a service. Putting words in their mouth is not.

Tell them where it will appear and for how long. Homepage, project page, a proposal. Named, with role and company. They may agree to one surface and not another. Honor that. A line cleared for a private proposal is not cleared for a paid ad. Get the wider use in writing if you want it. A short email is enough.

Do not ask them to lie about the relationship. If the project was narrow, the line should be narrow. A testimonial that implies they use you for everything, when you shipped one page, will embarrass both of you the moment a prospect calls them. Specificity is also a form of modesty. It keeps the claim inside the work.

## Name, role, and the real company

Put the person's name, their role, and the company. "A happy client" is an anonymous review, and anonymous reviews on your own site are a joke the buyer has seen before. If the person cannot be named, do not run the quote. Run the case study without a puppet attribution.

Use a likeness only with the same permission as the words. A photo they approved. Not a stock face. Not an illustration that implies a person you did not photograph. If you have no photo, type is enough. A well-set name under a specific sentence looks more trustworthy than a headshot that feels borrowed.

Check that the role is still true when you publish, and revisit it when you know it has changed. A quote from a job they left two years ago can stay if the work is unchanged and they are still willing, but the title should not pretend they are still there. Date the line if the context is time-bound. Undated superlatives age into fiction.

Logos next to quotes need the same permission as the words. A sentence they approved does not automatically approve a logo lockup in a sales deck, a booth, and a paid placement. Ask. The wall of logos is a separate decision, with its own way of going wrong.

## Layout that does not drown the line

The line is the content. The quotation mark, the giant faded initial, the five gold stars, and the carousel arrows are chrome. If the chrome is louder than the sentence, shrink the chrome. A reader should be able to read the words without feeling managed by a widget.

Do not auto-rotate testimonials. Rotation hides the line they were trying to read and treats proof as a billboard. Show the one or two lines you mean. If you have more, give them a project page each, next to the work. A library of specific quotes is a resource. A ticker of vague ones is a habit.

Set the quote in the text face, at a size you can read as a paragraph. Display type is for a short line that can survive it. A long quote in a theatrical face becomes a poster nobody finishes. Keep the attribution quieter than the quote, but still readable. Contrast applies here too. A pale gray name under a pale gray sentence fails the people you most want to inform.

One quote in a section is often the right number. Two, if they cover different situations a buyer might be in. Ten, in a grid, trains the eye to read none of them. Edit. The unused lines can live in a proposal where the situation matches. The homepage is not an archive of everyone who was nice.

## Permission, edits, and what you must not invent

You may tighten grammar with their approval. You may not upgrade the outcome, add a metric, or stitch two emails into a stronger opinion. The published line should be a subset of what they meant, not an improvement on it. Keep the original note. If a dispute or a simple question arises, you want the source.

Do not write a testimonial from a composite. Do not have the team "play the client" in an early draft that somehow ships. Do not buy a quote. A serious buyer may ask to speak with the person. The person should recognize the sentence. Google's guidance on people-first content treats trust as the heart of experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness. A faked customer is the opposite of that, and it is the kind of factual error a reader can check.

If a client wants to stay kind and general, thank them and do not publish. You can describe the project yourself, in your own voice, and mark it as your description. Your voice claiming a result is accountable in a way a puppet quote is not. Label studio notes as studio notes.

When a relationship ends, ask whether the line should stay. Some clients are happy to leave a true sentence up. Some are not. Take it down promptly if they ask. A testimonial is a living permission, not a trophy you captured.

## Where it sits in the sale

Place the line after the claim it supports. If you say you can move a store without breaking checkout, the quote near that claim should be about a store, not about a brand workshop. Mismatched proof is almost as weak as no proof. It suggests you have compliments and you are spending them at random.

Do not open the page with a quote if the quote is doing the job of the headline. The headline is your claim. The quote is someone else's confirmation. Leading with praise before you have said what you do forces the buyer to reverse-engineer the offer from a compliment. Say the offer. Then show that someone in that situation agrees.

In a proposal, choose the line that matches the prospect's situation, and quote it in full enough that you are not hiding context. A single flattering clause, cut out of a longer caveat, is a way of being specific and still misleading. Keep the caveat if it was part of the meaning. Mature buyers trust you more for it.

Hanabi would rather show the work than invent a chorus. Public projects can carry their own explanation. A quote, when it exists, should survive a founder reading it aloud to their co-founder without wincing. That is the editing standard. The layout comes after the sentence passes.

If you are about to ask a client for a line and you want the surrounding site to be worth their name, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the project you would want them to describe. The sentence gets easier when the work is clear.

A logo next to a quote can help or it can overclaim. [Logo walls and when to skip them](/blog/logo-walls-and-when-to-skip-them) is the next piece, on using marks you are allowed to show, at a size someone can read, or leaving the wall off.
